headline: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
name: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
description: scan-cycle model with idealized unbounded integers. The artifact that runs on the board, however, executes on a resource-constrained Microcontroller Unit (MCU) with a 16-bit machine word (8-bit AVR Arduinos), and sensors are read through a finite-resolution Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). We show that this deployment gap makes naive width-aware verification unsound in practice: on 123 real third-party programs, checking 16-bit arithmetic overflow without a hardware input model raises a 44 % false-alarm rate (54/123) and finds zero genuine defects, because it explores sensor values no ADC can produce. Because the gap sits exactly where computation meets the physical process – a bounded sensor reading scaled by finite-width integer arithmetic into an actuation command – an overflow can silently suppress a physical safety action such as a high-level alarm. At the same time, an unbounded input model fabricates alarms that no environment can trigger. We present a method for hardware-faithful verification of IEC 61131-3 on open hardware: a declarative Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) descriptor (word width, ADC/Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) resolution, I/O binding) and a sound lowering that interprets arithmetic at the target word width and constrains each input to its hardware-realizable range, transferring to the Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) domain the target-model discipline established for safety-critical embedded C (Frama-C, Astrée). We instantiate it for Arduino as ESBMC-Arduino, deriving HAL parameters from the official Arduino cores and realizing the input-range model as a lightweight hook in the Efficient SMT-based Context-Bounded Model Checker (ESBMC) Ladder Diagram (LD) frontend. On the 123-program corpus, the HAL annotator eliminates all 54 false alarms (54→0) while preserving every robustness proof, and a controlled corpus demonstrates the genuine – but rare – width-dependent defects the method detects with physically realizable witnesses.

hasPart.name: 1. Introduction
hasPart.description: Introduces the context of open-source PLCs and highlights the deployment gap between idealized verification models and resource-constrained hardware execution. It details the core contributions of the paper and outlines the scope of the research.

hasPart.name: 1.1 The Deployment Gap
hasPart.description: Explains the discrepancies that arise when transitioning from abstract verification models to physical microcontrollers with finite data widths and sensor resolutions.

hasPart.name: 1.2 Contributions
hasPart.description: Summarizes the primary technical advancements, tools, and formal methods introduced to bridge the deployment gap for open-hardware PLCs.

hasPart.name: 1.3 Scope
hasPart.description: Defines the boundaries of the study, specifying the types of hardware targets and verification frameworks considered in the evaluation.

hasPart.name: 2. Background
hasPart.description: Provides foundational concepts regarding the PLC scan cycle, open-hardware toolchains, PLCopen XML standards, and machine models for Arduino-class targets. It also reviews bounded model checking and k-induction techniques.

hasPart.name: 2.1 The PLC Scan Cycle
hasPart.description: Describes the standard operational loop of Programmable Logic Controllers, involving input reading, logic execution, and output updating.

hasPart.name: 2.2 Open-Hardware PLCs and the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Reviews open-source industrial hardware alternatives and the software toolchain used to compile IEC 61131-3 code into executable binaries.

hasPart.name: 2.4 PLCopen XML
hasPart.description: Outlines the XML-based exchange format used to represent PLC programs, configurations, and function blocks across different engineering tools.

hasPart.name: 2.5 From PLCopen XML to a Binary: the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Details the compilation pipeline that transforms high-level PLCopen XML representations into target-specific C/C++ code and machine binaries.

hasPart.name: 2.6 Machine Models of Arduino-Class Targets
hasPart.description: Examines the hardware architecture and memory constraints of microcontroller targets, focusing on word sizes and fixed-width data types.

hasPart.name: 2.7 Bounded Model Checking andk-Induction for PLCs
hasPart.description: Explains how formal verification algorithms like bounded model checking and k-induction are applied to verify safety properties in PLC software.

hasPart.name: 3. Related Work
hasPart.description: Surveys existing literature on the verification of IEC 61131-3 code, target-faithful analysis of embedded software, and code-generation correctness.

hasPart.name: 3.1 Verification of IEC 61131-3
hasPart.description: Discusses previous academic and industrial approaches aimed at verifying industrial control programs written in IEC 61131-3 languages.

hasPart.name: 3.2 Target-Faithful Analysis of Embedded Software
hasPart.description: Reviews methods that ensure software analysis tools account for specific hardware behaviors, such as compiler optimizations and integer overflow rules.

hasPart.name: 3.3 Code-Generation Correctness
hasPart.description: Examines research dedicated to proving that code generators and compilers preserve the semantic properties of the source specifications.

hasPart.name: 4. The Deployment Gap, Formally
hasPart.description: Formalizes the deployment gap by defining the physical process, fault models, assumptions, and presenting motivating examples of verification unsoundness.

hasPart.name: 4.1 Physical Process and Fault Model
hasPart.description: Defines the interaction between the physical environment and the controller, establishing the baseline fault model used for formal analysis.

hasPart.name: 4.1.1 Fault model
hasPart.description: Details the specific categories of hardware and software faults considered within the formal framework.

hasPart.name: 4.1.2 Assumptions
hasPart.description: Outlines the foundational assumptions regarding sensor behavior, actuator constraints, and execution environments.

hasPart.name: 4.1.3 Motivating example
hasPart.description: Presents a concrete case study illustrating how hardware limitations cause divergences between verified models and physical execution.

hasPart.name: 5. Hardware-Faithful Verification
hasPart.description: Proposes a hardware-faithful verification framework, detailing the scan-cycle execution model, faithful lowering techniques, and soundness diagnostics.

hasPart.name: 5.1 Scan-Cycle Execution Model
hasPart.description: Defines the formal semantics of the scan cycle adapted for hardware-faithful verification.

hasPart.name: 5.3 Faithful Lowering
hasPart.description: Describes the transformation process that maps high-level control semantics into hardware-accurate representations.

hasPart.name: 5.4 Soundness and Gap Diagnosis
hasPart.description: Analyzes the theoretical soundness of the proposed verification approach and introduces mechanisms to diagnose discrepancies caused by the deployment gap.

hasPart.name: 6.2 Implementation
hasPart.description: Details the software architecture, engineering decisions, placement of hooks, and configurability of the implemented verification framework.

hasPart.name: 6.2.1 Where the Hook Sits
hasPart.description: Explains the architectural placement of instrumentation hooks within the compilation and verification pipeline.

hasPart.name: 6.2.2 What the Hook Emits
hasPart.description: Describes the specific monitoring data and assertions generated by the hooks during verification.

hasPart.name: 6.2.3 Configurability and Engineering
hasPart.description: Discusses how engineers can configure verification parameters to suit different microcontroller targets and application requirements.

hasPart.name: 7. The Approach in Practice
hasPart.description: Demonstrates the practical application of the approach, contrasting the engineer's high-level view with internal execution mechanisms.

hasPart.name: 7.1.1 Engineer’s View
hasPart.description: Outlines how automation engineers interact with the tool and interpret verification outcomes in a real-world workflow.

hasPart.name: 7.1.2 Under the Hood
hasPart.description: Presents an in-depth look at the internal algorithms and intermediate representations driving the practical verification tool.

hasPart.name: 8. Evaluation
hasPart.description: Presents experimental results evaluating setup methodology, the frequency of the deployment gap, tool scalability, cross-tool validation, and overall performance.

hasPart.name: 8.1 Setup and Methodology
hasPart.description: Describes the benchmarks, hardware configurations, and experimental environment used to assess the verification framework.

hasPart.name: 8.2 RQ1: The Gap Is Real but Rare
hasPart.description: Evaluates research question 1, showing that while deployment gaps occur in practice, they appear infrequently across standard benchmark suites.

hasPart.name: 8.3 RQ2: Naive Width-Aware Verification Is Unusable
hasPart.description: Addresses research question 2 by demonstrating the computational impracticality and limitations of naive width-aware verification strategies.

hasPart.name: 8.4 RQ3: The HAL Annotator Restores Soundness
hasPart.description: Examines research question 3, proving that integrating the hardware abstraction layer annotator successfully recovers verification soundness.

hasPart.name: 8.5 Cross-Tool Validation: the Gap Is Not Tool-Specific
hasPart.description: Compares results across multiple verification engines to confirm that the deployment gap is a fundamental hardware-software issue rather than an artifact of a single tool.

hasPart.name: 10. Threats to Validity
hasPart.description: Identifies potential internal and external validity threats affecting the empirical study and discusses mitigation strategies.

hasPart.name: 11. Future Work
hasPart.description: Proposes avenues for future research, including expanding support to more complex architectures and advanced sensor models.

hasPart.name: 12. Conclusion
hasPart.description: Summarizes the paper's core contributions, emphasizing the importance of hardware-faithful verification in closing the deployment gap for open-hardware PLCs.

hasPart.name: 8.6 RQ4: Performance and Completeness
hasPart.description: Evaluates research question 4 regarding computational overhead, solving time, and completeness bounds of the proposed verification framework.

hasPart.name: 9. Discussion
hasPart.description: Reflects on the broader implications of the findings for industrial control system security and formal methods in embedded systems.
